946.title: The Armenian genocide (1915)
946.hook: Armenians, an old Christian people, are deported and killed under the Ottoman government; told carefully and honestly
946.howItsDone: The Armenian Apostolic Church honors the victims as saints, and Armenian communities gather each spring for services, processions and the laying of flowers to remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Christmas truce, when enemies sang carols across the trenches. Your line was silent night in no man's land. What did you hand across, and what came back? Day nine hundred forty-six.

A priest sits at a table with a notebook, writing down a song an old woman in a mountain village has just sung for him. A work song, sung while plowing. He's been walking from village to village, saving tunes that were never written down. His name is Komitas. He's an Armenian priest and a composer, and these songs are his people's memory. Then one night, during the First World War, he is arrested in Constantinople along with other Armenian leaders, writers and clergy. Some of them never come back. Today is a hard day in the story, and we'll go slowly.

The Armenians are an old Christian people, with their own church, their own alphabet and their own hymns, living in the lands of the Ottoman Empire. During the First World War, the Ottoman government arrested Armenian leaders, then forced whole Armenian communities from their homes. Men were often killed near their towns. Women, children and the old were marched toward the Syrian desert, and huge numbers died on the way, of killing, hunger, thirst and exhaustion. Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered in those years too. Historians who study these years, the Armenian churches, and the title of today's lesson call it genocide: an attempt to destroy a people. The government of Turkey disputes that word. Here we tell it as survivors and historians have recorded it, and we name that dispute rather than hide it. Two more true things belong in the telling. Survivors' accounts describe Turkish, Kurdish and Arab neighbors, Muslims, who hid Armenian families or took in orphans, sometimes at risk to themselves. And Komitas survived the arrests, but the horror broke him, and he never composed again. The songs he saved are still sung. There is a line in the Gospel of Matthew, about the children killed at Bethlehem, quoted from the prophet Jeremiah: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The Bible doesn't hurry past grief like that. It lets it stand. The Armenian Apostolic Church has named the victims martyrs and saints, and Armenian communities gather each spring to remember them. And on a cross, a dying thief once asked for the same thing: "Lord, remember me." Remembering isn't revenge. It's refusing to let people disappear.

Here's the practice: learn one Armenian name. Today, it's Komitas. Settle, and breathe. Say the name quietly: Komitas. A priest who walked mountain villages saving songs, and lost his own voice to grief. Picture the old woman singing to him while he writes. Then let your mind widen to the families on the roads, whose names you don't know. You don't have to feel anything in particular. Just hold them. If you pray, you can ask God to remember them. If you don't, let the name Komitas stand for all of them for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The Armenian genocide. The killing and deportation of Armenians under the Ottoman government during the First World War, which Armenians remember as martyrdom.
Your line: remember them. Today, tell one person the name Komitas and one true thing about him, so that the name travels a little farther. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Dorothy Day
947.hook: a journalist who starts the Catholic Worker, houses of hospitality for the poor
947.howItsDone: Catholic Worker communities still run houses of hospitality and farms, where volunteers live alongside guests, share meals, and keep a daily rhythm of prayer and work. Some parishes also organize the works of mercy through food pantries, prison visits and funeral ministries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Armenian genocide, told slowly and carefully. Your line was remember them. Did one Armenian name stay with you through the day? Day nine hundred forty-seven.

A pot of soup is on the stove in a cramped office in New York, and the line for it reaches out the door and down the block. The woman ladling it out used to write for radical newspapers. She has marched with socialists, been arrested with suffragists, and lived the bohemian life of the Greenwich Village crowd. Now she's a Catholic, which surprised her old friends, and she still runs a newspaper. Only this one is about the poor, and the office doubles as a kitchen. Anyone who's hungry can sit down. Today, the journalist who turned a newsroom into a house.
screen: `A NEWSROOM THAT IS ALSO A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Dorothy Day came into the Catholic Church as an adult, and she didn't leave her care for workers and the poor at the church door. She met a French wanderer and thinker named Peter Maurin, who had a plan he liked to recite out loud: people should feed the hungry, shelter the homeless, and do it themselves, face to face, not hand it all to an agency. Together they started a paper, The Catholic Worker, and then houses of hospitality, places where people with nowhere else to go could eat and sleep. Farms followed. The houses spread to other cities, run by volunteers who often lived there too. The plan came straight out of an old Christian list called the works of mercy. Most of the first list is in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus describes the judgment of the nations. In the King James Bible: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Naked and clothed, sick and visited, in prison and visited. The old catechisms call these the corporal works of mercy, the body works, and add one more from tradition: burying the dead. A second list, the spiritual works, includes teaching, counseling, comforting, forgiving and praying. Day treated the lists as a job description. She also wrote and argued, against war and for workers, and she went to jail for her protests. She lived in the houses herself, poor among the poor. People who knew her describe her as fierce and impatient as well as kind. And she is remembered for brushing off the word saint, so that nobody could use it to dismiss what she did as too hard for ordinary people. The Catholic Church has since opened her cause for sainthood anyway.
screen: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer hospitality, starting with the idea of it. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself where your own door is. A table. A couch. A desk at work. A seat next to you on the bus. Then bring to mind someone who might need a place at it. A new coworker eating alone. A neighbor who doesn't get visitors. A friend between apartments. Don't plan anything big. Day's houses started with a pot of soup. Just let one face come to mind, and one small welcome you could offer them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Dorothy Day. A journalist who became a Catholic and, with Peter Maurin, started the Catholic Worker and its houses of hospitality.
Your line: the works of mercy. Today, do one of them with your own hands: a meal shared, a visit made, a coat passed on, a person welcomed in. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

948.title: Barmen (1934)
948.hook: Protestant Christians of the Confessing Church declare that Christ, not Hitler, is Lord
948.carry: jesus christ is the one word
948.howItsDone: Some Lutheran, Reformed and united Protestant churches include the Barmen Declaration among their confessional documents, and it is read and studied in congregations, especially when churches discuss faith and political power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dorothy Day, a pot of soup and a house with the door open. Your line was the works of mercy. Which one did you do with your own hands? Day nine hundred forty-eight.

Swastika flags hang inside some German churches. A movement calling itself the German Christians wants the Protestant church folded into the new state, wants a national bishop loyal to Hitler, and wants pastors of Jewish descent pushed out. Some pastors go along. Others don't. They gather in a church in Barmen, an industrial town on the Wupper river, Lutherans, Reformed and United side by side, and they write a short statement. It doesn't name Hitler once. It doesn't need to. Today, the town where a few Christians wrote down who their Lord was.

The group that met at Barmen came to be called the Confessing Church, because what they did was confess, in the old sense: say out loud what they believed. The theologian Karl Barth did much of the drafting. The declaration is built in a simple pattern. First a Bible verse, then a statement of faith, then a sentence that begins, in effect, we reject the false teaching. The first article opens with the words of Jesus in John's Gospel. In the King James Bible: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." Then comes the line today's carry is drawn from: Jesus Christ, as the Bible bears witness to him, is the one Word of God that the church must hear, trust and obey, in life and in death. And then the rejection: the church may not treat any other event, power, figure or truth as God's revelation alongside him. Read that in a country where some church voices were hailing the leader as a gift from God, and you can hear what it's saying without a single name. The term Word matters here. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word," and calls Jesus that Word. Barmen leans on it: one Word, not one Word plus a nation, a race or a leader. Now the honest part. Barmen defended the church's freedom to preach Christ. It said nothing directly about the Jews being driven from their jobs and homes, and later Christians, including some who were there, came to see that silence as a failure. Barmen is still read in churches today, often by Lutheran and Reformed Christians, as a model of saying no. It is also read as a reminder of what saying no left out.
screen: `TO CONFESS: TO SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say who is lord for you. Lord here just means the thing that gets the final say. Settle, and breathe. Ask what actually decides things in your life when it's hard. Money. Fear. What people will think. A boss. A belief. Don't judge the answer, just notice it. Then ask what you would want to have the final say. If you pray, you can say the words from John quietly: I am the way, the truth, and the life. If you don't, just name, in a few words, the one thing you won't hand over to anyone. The bell holds the time.
Barmen. The German town where the Confessing Church declared that Jesus Christ alone, and no state or leader, is the Word the church must obey.
Your line: jesus christ is the one word. Today, notice one voice that asks for more loyalty than it's owed, and say a small, polite no to it. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: The cost of discipleship
949.hook: Dietrich Bonhoeffer warns against cheap grace, grace without discipleship
949.howItsDone: The Cost of Discipleship is read in church study groups and seminaries across denominations, often alongside the Sermon on the Mount, which takes up much of the book.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barmen, and a few pastors who wrote down who their Lord was. Your line was jesus christ is the one word. What voice asked you for too much loyalty? Day nine hundred forty-nine.

Clearance sale. Everything must go. Grace, forgiveness, comfort, all marked down to nothing, no questions asked. That's roughly the picture a young German pastor painted of his own church. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran, from a church built on the teaching that God's grace is free, a gift nobody can earn. He held to that. And still he said the church had started giving grace away the wrong way, like stock it was trying to clear. He had a name for it. Today, the book where he named it.

Bonhoeffer was teaching young pastors for the Confessing Church, the church that had said no at Barmen, in a small seminary the government would later close. Out of that teaching came a book. In English it's called The Cost of Discipleship. In German it has one word for a title, Nachfolge, which means following after. It opens with two kinds of grace. Cheap grace, he wrote, is grace we hand ourselves. Forgiveness without turning around. Church membership without following. Grace without the cross, without Jesus, a doctrine we nod at and then go on living exactly as before. Costly grace is the other kind. He reached for Jesus's short parable in Matthew. In the King James Bible: "the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field." Notice the joy. The man isn't paying a fine. He's found something worth everything. That's costly grace: still a gift, never earned, but a gift that calls you to follow. Bonhoeffer put it in a pair of phrases that people still repeat: it is costly because it costs a life, and it is grace because it gives a life. Jesus said something close in Luke: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?" Christians have argued about the book ever since. Some hear a needed alarm. Others worry it leans too hard on effort and forgets the comfort of grace. Bonhoeffer himself said later that he could see dangers in it, though he stood by it. What makes it hard to brush off is what he did next. He kept following, right into the danger.
screen: `IT COSTS A LIFE, IT GIVES A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the costly good thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one good thing you already know you should do and keep putting off because it will cost you something. An apology that means admitting you were wrong. A call that will take an hour. Speaking up in a meeting. Giving something you'd rather keep. Don't decide anything yet. Just look at it honestly, and notice what the cost actually is. Then notice whether there's a field with treasure behind it. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
The cost of discipleship. Bonhoeffer's book on following Jesus, and his warning against cheap grace: grace that asks nothing and changes nothing.
Your line: not cheap grace. Today, do the costly good thing you pictured, or one honest step toward it. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Bonhoeffer's end (1945)
950.hook: executed weeks before liberation; his prison letters still read worldwide
950.howItsDone: Bonhoeffer is remembered on the calendars of several churches, including Lutheran and Anglican ones, and his prison letters and poems are read in study groups, sermons and private devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's book and his warning. Your line was not cheap grace. Did you take a step toward the costly good thing, or just look at it? Either counts. Day nine hundred fifty.

Prisoner Bonhoeffer, get ready to come with us. That, by one account, is what the guards said, at the door of a schoolroom where a group of prisoners was being held near the end of the war. The pastor had just led a short Sunday service for the others. He took a book, wrote his name in it, and asked one of the men, a British officer, to carry a message to a friend in England if he could. Then he went with the guards. The officer remembered the message. Today, the end of Dietrich Bonhoeffer's life, and the words he left behind.

Bonhoeffer was arrested at his parents' house in Berlin and held for a long time in a military prison. Through family and friends, he had become connected to people who were plotting against Hitler, and after a failed attempt on Hitler's life, those connections were uncovered. Christians still talk about this honestly. A man who wrote about following Jesus and was drawn toward peace joined, in some way, a conspiracy to kill a tyrant. Some see it as costly obedience in an impossible time. Others hold it as a hard question that doesn't resolve. In prison, he wrote. Letters to his parents, to his fiancée, Maria, and to his closest friend, Eberhard Bethge, who later gathered them into a book. They're full of ordinary things, a request for books, thanks for a parcel, and full of big questions about God and faith in a world that seemed to go on without either. He also wrote poems. In one he asks who he really is: the calm man the guards see, or the restless one he knows inside, and ends by placing the question with God. Near the end he was moved to the concentration camp at Flossenbürg and hanged there, shortly before the war in Europe ended. The message the British officer carried was short. As he remembered it, Bonhoeffer said: this is the end, for me the beginning of life. That echoes an old Christian hope, which Paul puts this way in the King James Bible: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" The letters are still read today. People who share none of his faith read them too, for the honesty.
screen: `WHO AM I? A QUESTION GIVEN TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write to someone you won't see soon. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is far away, by distance, by time, or by a falling-out. A grandparent. An old friend. A cousin overseas. Bonhoeffer's letters mixed small news with big things. So start a letter in your head with something ordinary: what you ate, what you're reading. Then add one sentence that matters, the thing you'd want them to know if this were your last letter. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you write. The bell holds the time.
Bonhoeffer's end. A pastor executed by the Nazi state, who left behind prison letters and, by one account, called his death the beginning of life.
Your line: the beginning of life. Today, send the letter, or a message, to the person you pictured: something ordinary, and one sentence that matters. Day nine hundred fifty.

951.title: The churches and the Holocaust
951.hook: Christians were among the silent and the complicit; a few, like the villagers of Le Chambon, hid Jews
951.howItsDone: Some churches now keep Holocaust Remembrance Day or Yom HaShoah services, often with local Jewish communities, and teach their members the history of Christian anti-Judaism alongside the stories of rescuers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's end, and a last message carried to a friend. Your line was the beginning of life. Did your letter go out? Day nine hundred fifty-one.

A knock at a farmhouse door, high on a cold plateau in the south of France. Outside, a stranger with a small suitcase, sometimes a child with no parents at all. Inside, a Protestant farming family who know what it is to be hunted, because their own church remembers a long history of persecution. They open the door. Across the plateau, around the village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, families did that again and again, and Jewish refugees were hidden in homes, farms and schools. This story has to be told next to a much harder one. Today, the churches and the Holocaust.

Here is the hard story first, said plainly. The Nazi state and those who helped it murdered Jews across Europe on a scale that is hard to hold in the mind. It happened in countries full of churches. Christians were among the silent, and Christians were among the complicit: people who looked away, people who informed, people who took part. And behind it lay a long history of Christian contempt for Jews, sermons and laws and slanders, including the false charge that the Jewish people as a whole were guilty of Jesus's death. Since the war, churches have said this out loud. The Catholic Church and other churches have formally rejected that charge, and some have asked forgiveness for the contempt that helped prepare the ground. Now the few. On the plateau, the pastor André Trocmé and his wife Magda helped lead their parish in sheltering refugees. Tradition says that when officials demanded names, the village answered that they didn't know any Jews, only people. Elsewhere there were others: a farmer, a nun, a bishop, a teenager carrying forged papers. Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, honors rescuers like these with a title, Righteous Among the Nations, and it has honored the people of that plateau. The rescuers weren't the rule. That's why we know their names. An old proverb in the King James Bible names what they refused to do: "If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain; If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?" We knew it not. People said that afterward. The few who hid them could never say it. They opened the door and knew exactly what it might cost.

Here's the practice: learn about one rescuer, starting with a question. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what you know about the people who hid others in those years. Maybe a name or two. Maybe nothing yet. Either is a fair place to start. Then let the hard part sit beside it: the people who were not hidden, and the homes that stayed closed. Don't hurry past it. If you pray, you can pray for the dead. If you don't, just stay with both for the length of the bell. Later today, look up one rescuer, the Trocmés or someone else, and read their story to the end. The bell holds the time.
The churches and the Holocaust. A history of silence, complicity and contempt, and beside it, a few Christians who hid Jews at great risk.

segments.voice: Your line: the few who hid them. Today, when you notice someone being talked about as less than human, don't say we knew it not. Say one quiet word for them. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

952.title: Maximilian Kolbe
952.hook: in Auschwitz a Polish priest offers his life in place of a father of a family
952.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Maximilian Kolbe each August, and he is honored as a patron of prisoners and families; his story is often told at Masses and in schools that bear his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the churches and the Holocaust: the silence, and beside it, the few who hid them. Whose rescue story did you read? Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Roll call in Auschwitz, in summer heat. A prisoner from the block has escaped, and the rule is brutal: men from his block will be chosen to die by starvation in an underground cell. The SS officer in charge walks the rows and points. One of the men picked, a Polish soldier named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cries out for his wife and his children. Then a thin prisoner in glasses steps out of line and walks toward the officer. Today, the man who stepped out.

The man was Maximilian Kolbe, a Polish Catholic priest and a Franciscan friar. Before the war he ran a large friary near Warsaw and printed magazines and newspapers, a busy, inventive man devoted to Mary. The Nazis arrested him, and he ended up in Auschwitz, a prisoner with a number instead of a name. At the roll call, by the accounts of survivors, he asked to take the place of the man with a family. When asked who he was, he said simply that he was a Catholic priest. The officer agreed. Gajowniczek went back into the line, and Kolbe went down into the starvation cell with the others. Witnesses later said that the cell, instead of screaming, was full of prayers and hymns, and that Kolbe led them. He was among the last still alive, and the guards killed him by lethal injection. Gajowniczek survived the camp and spent the rest of his life telling people what had been done for him. The Catholic Church has named Kolbe a saint, and the Gospel reading people often connect with him is from John. In the King James Bible: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Kolbe hadn't been the man's friend. By the accounts, they were strangers. Now look back at this week. Remember them, for the Armenians. The works of mercy. One Word, not a leader. Not cheap grace. The beginning of life. The few who hid them. And now, let me go instead. A week of people who paid a cost.
screen: `HE ASKS TO TAKE THE FATHER'S PLACE.`
`A WEEK OF PEOPLE WHO PAID A COST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take someone's place in a small thing. Nobody is asking for Kolbe's sacrifice. Start much smaller. Settle, and breathe. Look at the next day or two. Who is carrying something you could carry instead? The colleague with the dull task. The parent who always does bedtime. The friend who always drives. The neighbor who takes out everyone's bins. Pick one. Picture yourself stepping out of line and saying, quietly, let me do that one. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on them. The bell holds the time.
Maximilian Kolbe. A Polish friar who, in Auschwitz, asked to die in place of a man with a family, and was allowed to.
Your line: let me go instead. Today, take one small turn that belongs to someone else, and don't make a thing of it. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

pairs: than to lay down his life

myth: Kolbe and Gajowniczek were close friends
by the accounts, they were strangers. he asked to take the place of a man with a family.
the man Kolbe replaced survived the camp
Gajowniczek survived and spent his life telling what had been done for him.
Kolbe was a quiet hermit before the war
he ran a large friary and printed magazines and newspapers.

fork.setup: you're standing in the rows. a stranger next to you has just been chosen to die, and he's crying for his children. what do you do?
options: keep your eyes down and stay in line.
step out and ask to take his place.
whisper a prayer for him and stay still.
fork.reveal: Kolbe stepped out, said he was a Catholic priest, and asked to take the father's place. the officer agreed.

original.note: Greek: for, on behalf of, in place of. John 15:13, lay down his life for his friends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hero who did a brave thing once.
what it means: a friar who asked to die in a stranger's place, and led prayers in the starvation cell.
what a scholar hears: the account rests on survivors and on Gajowniczek himself, and the Church named Kolbe a martyr of charity.

sources.ref: survivor testimony, including Franciszek Gajowniczek; standard biographies of Maximilian Kolbe
